clue.text: Katharine acted chirpily in Reagan country

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase standing for the American insect named after its chirping call

parts.note: Katy is a pet form of the name Katharine
to act is to do, so acted gives did

explanation.surface: An actress called Katharine gives a bright, chirpy performance somewhere in Ronald Reagan's America.
explanation.walkthrough: Reagan country is the USA, where the katydid, a large green grasshopper, is named from its call, which seems to say 'Katy did'. The definition is loose: it points at what chirps there rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: The katydid is a North American bush cricket whose chirping call gives it its name.

clue.text: A great power-house in Moscow

parts.note: read as a building in Moscow that houses great political power, the seat of Russian government

explanation.surface: A big power station somewhere in the Russian capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moscow citadel is the seat of the Russian government, so it literally houses great power.

clue.text: Be afraid to consider what 9 might do if any screws loose

definitions.meaning: to dread even thinking about something

definitions.text: what 9 might do if any screws loose
definitions.meaning: a computer with loose screws would rattle and shake while it worked

explanation.surface: A warning about dreading the thought of a machine that has come loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is ELECTRONIC BRAIN, the computer; a thinking machine with loose screws would literally shake as it thinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to dread contemplating something; a rickety computer would literally shudder when calculating.

clue.text: Service tax

definitions.meaning: a spell of work or obligation, as in being on guard
a levy, as on imported goods

explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both an obligation or spell of service and a levy charged on goods.

clue.text: Many rascals show which way the wind is blowing

definitions.text: show which way the wind is blowing
definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the plural noun: the things that show the wind's direction

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a crossword stand-in for many
rogues are rascals

explanation.surface: A gang of scoundrels reveals the way public opinion is heading.
explanation.walkthrough: Drogues are windsocks, the cloth cones at airfields that show the wind direction; the definition describes what they do.
explanation.definitionFit: A drogue is a windsock, a fabric cone flown at airfields to indicate wind direction.

clue.text: Prison putting tragic end to one's years

indicators.note: the end of the word tragic is its final letter

parts.note: the number of years one has lived is one's age

explanation.surface: A grim jail sentence that brings a sad close to someone's life.
explanation.definitionFit: A cage is an enclosure for confining a captive, a prison in miniature.

clue.text: The chest protector that helps artificial respiration

definitions.meaning: a piece of armour covering the torso
a respirator worn around the chest that pumps air into the lungs

explanation.definitionFit: It is both a breastplate of armour and the name of a chest-worn respirator for assisted breathing.

clue.text: One marsh turned to stone and sand in China

indicators.note: turned means the two words one and marsh are read back to front as a single run

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a bog is a marsh

explanation.surface: A wetland that has somehow turned to rock and sand somewhere in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses I + BOG as one run to give GOBI. 'turned to stone' looks like petrification but 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gobi is the great stony and sandy desert of northern China and Mongolia.

clue.text: Cutler's case may pre, the Alicante enquiry

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Cutler's case may pre, the Alicante enquiry': CANTEEN is hidden in 'Alicante enquiry' but the words 'may pre, the' are garbled OCR and no hidden-word indicator survives.
annotationWithheld.clue: Cutler's case may pre, the Alicante enquiry

clue.text: Perhaps the doorstep sales man's calling for her, but usually mum's the word!

definitions.text: Perhaps the doorstep sales man's calling for her, but usually mum's the word!

parts.words: Perhaps the doorstep sales man's calling for her, but usually mum's the word!
parts.note: a salesman at the door asks for the woman in charge of the home, who is usually the mother; 'mum's the word' also means keeping quiet

explanation.surface: A door-to-door salesman asks for a woman, though the household keeps quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the woman who runs a household, the person a salesman traditionally asks for.

clue.text: One automatically thinks of cerebral tonic in shake-up

indicators.note: a shake-up jumbles the order, so the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who thinks only on autopilot after a brain tonic has been shaken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One automatically thinks' reads like a description of a person on autopilot, but it defines a machine. The 'in' before 'shake-up' is part of the letters to be jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: An old term for a computer: a machine that carries out thinking-like processes automatically.

clue.text: Where, a hanger-on gets attached to one of her listeners?

definitions.text: Where, a hanger-on gets attached to one of her listeners?

parts.words: Where, a hanger-on gets attached to one of her listeners?
parts.note: the hanger-on is a dangling earring, and her listeners are her ears; the place it hooks on is the soft lower part of the ear

explanation.surface: A clingy follower latches on to one of the people listening to a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The fleshy lower part of the ear is where an earring is hung.

clue.text: Once a golden contribution to Europe's education

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase standing for the noun: a gold coin of former times

indicators.note: a contribution is a part given to the whole, so the letters are a part found within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something that once enriched European schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'Europe's education', inside 'eDUCATion'. The definition is clipped: 'Once a golden' leaves 'coin' understood.
explanation.definitionFit: The ducat was a gold coin used across Europe in former centuries.

clue.text: Lower dwelling in Scotland

parts.note: a lower is something that lows, a cow, so this is a cow's home, using a Scottish and northern word

explanation.surface: A humble cottage in the Scottish lowlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' reads as 'less high' but means 'one that lows', a cow.
explanation.definitionFit: A byre is a cowshed, the term used in Scotland and northern England.

clue.text: First list of candidates for economics school disturbed at heart

indicators.note: at heart means the word at is placed in the middle of the other letters
disturbed letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: LSE is the London School of Economics

explanation.surface: An initial shortlist for a university that is troubled deep down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' jumbles LSE to SLE, and 'at heart' puts AT in its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A slate is a list of candidates put forward for election.

clue.text: Mean do-it-yourself? Get right in!

indicators.note: get in means one piece is put inside the other

explanation.surface: Someone stingy tells you to do the job yourself and get stuck in.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirty trick is a mean, low one; both words describe dishonourable behaviour.

clue.text: Does the sailor thread his way through them?

definitions.text: Does the sailor thread his way through them?

parts.words: Does the sailor thread his way through them?
parts.note: threading suggests sewing tools, but a sailor steers among rocks of that name

explanation.surface: A question about whether a seaman sews his way through something.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are a line of chalk rocks off the Isle of Wight, in southern England, that sailors must navigate past.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sewing tools and also the rocks off the Isle of Wight that sailors pass.

clue.text: Feeling limp? Add more starch and iron

definitions.text: Feeling limp? Add more starch and iron

parts.words: Feeling limp? Add more starch and iron
parts.note: reads as diet advice for someone weak, but describes laundry treatment that makes fabric rigid

explanation.surface: Health advice: if you're feeling feeble, take more carbohydrate and iron.
explanation.definitionFit: Starching and pressing make limp fabric rigid; the answer means to make firm.

clue.text: Stood everyone a drink and made sure they all heard about it

definitions.meaning: bought a round, using the British and Australian slang for paying for drinks

definitions.text: made sure they all heard about it

explanation.surface: Someone buys the whole bar a round and makes a loud fuss about it.
explanation.walkthrough: In British and Australian slang, a 'shout' is your turn to buy a round of drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both treated people to drinks and yelled so that everyone heard.

clue.text: Regional railway coppers in double-breasted top wear

indicators.note: in means the coins go inside the railway's letters

parts.note: SR is the Southern Region of British Railways
coppers are copper coins, pence

explanation.surface: Railway police wearing double-breasted jackets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coppers' suggests police, but means copper coins, PENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A spencer is a short close-fitting jacket or overcoat, a garment worn on the upper body.

clue.text: Aped and messed about without expression

indicators.note: messed about means the letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone mimicked and fooled around while keeping a straight face.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan face shows no emotion; it is blank and impassive.

clue.text: Through maddening urge landed in jug

indicators.note: landed in means one piece is set down inside the other

parts.note: per means through, as in per post
an itch is a maddening urge

explanation.surface: A maddening craving got someone thrown into jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jug' is slang for prison in the surface, but here it means a pouring vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitcher is a large jug for pouring liquids.

clue.text: A feat for vingt-et-un

definitions.meaning: in the card game, a winning two-card hand of an ace and a picture card counts as a notable achievement
the French name of the card game also called twenty-one or blackjack

explanation.walkthrough: Pontoon is the British name for the card game vingt-et-un, and also for its best hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The name covers both the card game twenty-one and its top hand, an ace with a court card.

clue.text: Favour a bunch of ribbons?

definitions.meaning: a badge or knot of ribbon worn to show support
ribbons gathered into a circular decoration

explanation.definitionFit: A rosette is a ribbon badge given or worn as a favour, made of gathered ribbons.

clue.text: Reflect on the word, perhaps

parts.note: reads as 'think about the word', but means bounce back a spoken word

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to ponder a word.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo reflects sound back, so a spoken word is repeated to the speaker.

clue.text: Heavenly food dropped round an awkward man

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go around the other word
awkward signals that the letters of man are put in an ungainly new order

explanation.surface: Food from heaven falls around a clumsy fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' jumbles the man to MNA, and 'round' wraps that around AN. 'dropped' belongs with the definition, recalling manna falling from heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: In Exodus, manna was the food dropped from heaven to feed the Israelites in the wilderness.

clue.text: Welshman-may be called to put year in society of rowing initially

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Welshman-may be called to put year in society of rowing initially': Y goes in RHS, but 'society of rowing initially' supplies no H, so the OCR text is garbled.
annotationWithheld.clue: Welshman-may be called to put year in society of rowing initially

clue.text: Measure a boundary

definitions.meaning: to measure out or allot, as in to dole out punishment
an old word for a limit

explanation.definitionFit: It is a verb for allotting or measuring out and an archaic noun for a boundary marker.

clue.text: A flat-bottomed boat from Cowes losing Oriental character

indicators.note: from signals that the letters of the town are reworked to make the boat, with one dropped

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for east, the Orient

explanation.surface: A flat boat sailing out of Cowes, having lost its eastern flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowes is a sailing town on the Isle of Wight. 'losing' drops E from COWES, and the remaining COWS is reworked to give SCOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A scow is a broad flat-bottomed boat, used for freight or as a lighter.

clue.text: But" it wouldn't mean a jail sentence for John McEnroe

definitions.text: But" it wouldn't mean a jail sentence for John McEnroe

parts.words: But" it wouldn't mean a jail sentence for John McEnroe
parts.note: the tennis player was famous for showing scorn on the tennis court, which would not be the legal offence that leads to prison

explanation.surface: A comment that a hot-tempered tennis star would escape imprisonment.
explanation.walkthrough: John McEnroe was a US tennis player known for outbursts at umpires; his scorn on court is not the legal offence.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal offence of disrespecting a judge or court, punishable by jail, is turned into scorn shown on a tennis court.

clue.text: Average fellows, about middle-class?

indicators.note: about signals that the word for fellows goes around the other letter

parts.note: fellows are men

indicators.note: the central letter of the word class is wanted here

explanation.surface: Ordinary blokes, roughly middle-class?
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle-class' looks like a social grade but asks for the central letter of 'class', A, placed inside MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The mean is the arithmetical average of a set of values.

clue.text: Hasn't-any clothes, we hear, " so isn't in the running

indicators.note: we hear means the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: having no clothes means no wear

explanation.surface: A naked runner is not in contention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no wear', having no clothes, sounds the same as NOWHERE; a horse placed nowhere is out of the running.
explanation.definitionFit: To be nowhere in a race is to be unplaced, out of contention.
